analytic.title: Exact response-time analysis for fixed-priority preemption-threshold scheduling

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Fixed-priority preemption-threshold scheduling (FPTS) has been proposed as a generalization of fixedpriority preemptive scheduling (FPPS) and fixed-priority nonpreemptive scheduling (FPNS) with the aim to improve schedulability and reduce run-time overheads. In this paper, we show that the existing worst-case response time (WCRT) analysis for FPTS is pessimistic and present an exact WCRT analysis. Moreover, we refine the task model for FPTS, making FPTS also a generalization of fixed-priority scheduling with deferred preemption (FPDS). Finally, we present exact analysis for FPTS for this refined task model and an example showing that FPTS can improve on FPPS and FPDS.

div.head: A. Background
div.p: Fixed-priority preemption threshold scheduling (FPTS) was first introduced in a commercial real-time operating system ThreadX [1] with the aim to improve schedulability and reduce run-time overheads compared to fixed-priority preemptive scheduling (FPPS). In FPTS, each task has a preemption threshold P next to its regular priority P, where the preemption threshold is higher than or equal to its priority. While a task is executing, only tasks with a priority higher than the preemption threshold of that task can preempt. FPTS generalizes both FPPS and fixed-priority non-preemptive scheduling (FPNS); by selecting P = P for all tasks we get FPPS and by selecting P equal to the highest priority for all tasks we get FPNS.

Worst-case response time (WCRT) analysis for FPTS was first presented in [2], including an efficient algorithm to determine optimal preemption threshold assignments. In [3], it is shown that the analysis in [2] was optimistic, and a revised analysis was presented.

div.head: B. Motivation
div.p: We revisit the existing analysis for FPTS for two reasons. Firstly, the analysis presented in [3] is uniform, whereas the exact analysis for fixed-priority scheduling with deferred preemption (FPDS) presented in [5] is not uniform, i.e. the analysis for the lowest priority task differs from the analysis of other tasks. Given the fact that FPNS is a specialization of FPDS, one would expect that the analysis of FPTS presented in [3] would not be uniform either.

Secondly, FPTS generalizes FPPS and FPNS. Given the fact that FPDS generalizes FPNS, we would like to extend FPTS in such a way that it generalizes FPPS and FPDS, i.e. by refining the task model. Such a generalization is particularly attractive for systems as described in [4], where mode-change latencies play an important role, i.e. the leadtime from a mode-change request till the time the modechange can be actuated. In [4], it has been shown that, compared to FPPS, FPDS can significantly reduce the modechange latency of systems. This reduction is an immediate consequence of the limited preemptability of tasks scheduled by means of FPDS. However, many systems are not schedulable by means of FPDS. For these systems, we would like to trade mode-change latencies for schedulability. By refining the task model for FPTS, FPTS can provide the scheduling means we are aiming for.

div.head: C. Contributions
div.p: We show that the existing WCRT analysis for FPTS is pessimistic (Section IV) and present an exact WCRT analysis (Section V) that specializes to the WCRT analysis of FPNS. Moreover, we refine the task model for FPTS by assuming that each task consists of a sequence of subjobs (Section II). Finally, we present exact analysis for FPTS for our refined task model (Section VI), making FPTS a generalization of FPPS and FPDS and an example showing that FPTS can improve on FPPS and FPDS (Section VII).

div.head: II. REAL-TIME SCHEDULING MODEL AND NOTATION
div.p: We assume a single processor and a set T of n periodically released, independent tasks τ 1 , τ 2 , . . ., τ n with unique, fixed priorities P 1 , P 2 , . . ., P n . For notational convenience, we assume that (i) tasks are given in order of decreasing priorities, i.e. τ 1 has highest priority and τ n has lowest priority, and (ii) a higher priority is represented by a lower value, i.e. P 1 < P 2 < . . . < P n . We now present a basic and a refined task model for FPTS.

div.head: A. Basic task model for FPTS
div.p: Each task τ i is characterized by a (release) period T i ∈ R + , an activation jitter J i ∈ R + ∪ {0}, a worst-case computation time C i ∈ R + , a (relative) deadline D i ∈ R + , where C i ≤ D i ≤ T i -J i , and a phasing ϕ i ∈ R + ∪ {0}. We assume arbitrary phasing for tasks. A release of a task is termed a job.

For FPTS, each task τ i has a preemption threshold P i next to its priority P i , where P i ≤ P i . When τ i is executing, it can only be preempted by tasks with a priority higher than P i . Note that FPTS specializes to (i) FPPS when P i = P i for all i and to (ii) FPNS when P i = P 1 for all i.

div.head: B. Refined task model for FPTS
div.p: In the refined task model, each job of task τ i is assumed to consist of a sequence of m i subjobs. The k th subjob of τ i is characterized by a worst-case computation time
div.formula: C ik ∈ R + , where C i = ∑ m i k=1 C ik .
div.p: For FPTS, preemption thresholds are associated with subjobs rather than tasks1 . The k th subjob of τ i has preemption threshold P ik , where P ik ≤ P i . When the k th subjob of τ i is executing, it can only be preempted by tasks with a priority higher than P ik . At subjob boundaries, τ i can still be preempted by any higher priority task. Note that when m i = 1 for all i, we have the basic task model as special case of our refined task model. Further note that FPTS specializes to FPDS when P ik = P 1 for all i, k.

div.head: IV. EXISTING WCRT ANALYSIS IS PESSIMISTIC
div.p: In this section, the WCRT analysis for FPTS presented in [3] will be investigated by means of an example task set that consists of three tasks. The timing and priority characteristics of the task set T I are given in Table I.

If we use the WCRT analysis recapitulated in Section III, we find R 2 = 8, which means that T I is not schedulable. Figure 1 illustrates the timeline for T I relating the worstcase scenario to reach R 2 . In this scenario, τ 3 is released an infinitesimal amount of time (ε > 0) before the release of τ 1 and τ 2 . These first two tasks are blocked by τ 3 because no preemption is allowed. After the execution of τ 3 at (3ε), the first job of τ 1 starts running and it completes the execution at time (5 -ε). Then the first job of τ 2 starts running. The second job of τ 1 that arrives at time 5 cannot preempt τ 2 , so τ 2 completes its execution at time (6 -ε). Since lim ε↓0 (6 -ε) = 6, we therefore find a supremum (not a maximum) equal to 6 for R 2 . The existing analysis for FPTS is therefore pessimistic.

The pessimism results from the S ik expression given by (4) that yields S 2,0 = 7 for the example. Yet, the timeline analysis reveals that S 2,0 is equal to (5 -ε). In fact, the existing analysis does not take into account that τ i can only be blocked by a lower priority task if that task starts executing before the simultaneous release of τ i and higher priority tasks.

div.head: VII. MODE CHANGES BASED ON FPTS
div.p: In [4], a mode change can only be actuated when all tasks involved in that mode change are at a subjob boundary. The mode-change latency therefore is the longest time it takes for the executing subjobs of all involved tasks to complete. For FPDS, the mode change latency is minimal, i.e. determined by the longest subjob of the involved tasks.

In the following example we trade the mode-change latency for schedulability by using FPTS. It is shown that FPTS can have an advantage over FPDS considering the schedulability. The example relates such a case: task set T III , consisting of three tasks involved in a mode change, is not schedulable under FPPS, FPNS and FPDS whereas it is schedulable under FPTS. T III is constructed by modifying the task set given in [2] and partitioning the tasks into the subjobs. Table III gives the timing characteristics of T III . Under FPDS the task set is not schedulable because of τ 1 whereas under FPTS the first job of τ 1 finishes before its deadline by preempting τ 3 . Note that while τ 3 is not schedulable under FPPS, it can meet its deadline under FPTS because the subjobs of τ 3 cannot be preempted by τ 2 based on the preemption thresholds given in Table III.

Yet, making T III schedulable by using FPTS results in longer mode-change latency compared to FPDS. For the example, the mode-change latency can be 3.1 under FPDS that is the longest execution time among subjobs of all tasks. Under FPTS it increases to 3.1 + 2 = 5.1 due to the preemption by τ 1 . Thus, the task set is made schedulable at the expense of a longer latency for the mode change.

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSION
div.p: In [1], [2], FPTS has been proposed as a generalization of FPPS and FPNS, with the aim to improve schedulability and reduce run-time overheads. In this paper, we showed that the existing WCRT analysis for FPTS [3] is pessimistic because the blocking time is a supremum for the tasks with a positive worst-case blocking time rather than a maximum. We presented an exact WCRT analysis. Moreover, we refined the task model for FPTS, making FPTS a generalization of FPDS, and presented exact WCRT analysis for FPTS for this refined task model.

We aim at applying FPTS in systems where mode-change latencies play an important role. Whenever such systems are not schedulable by means of FPDS, FPTS may be an attractive alternative, trading mode-change latency for schedulability, which we illustrated by means of an example.

Two main issues remain as future work. Firstly, we identified an option to further generalize the task model, i.e. to have a preemption threshold for a task and preemption thresholds for subjobs, but the corresponding analysis is still open. Secondly, we aim at deriving an algorithm to minimize the mode-change latency for a given system using preemption thresholds.
